question: The Lectures on Faith, bound with the Doctrine and Covenants from 1835, were removed from the standard edition in 1921. From a doctrinally-aware standpoint, what is the most accurate characterization of Lecture 5's teaching on the Godhead and why its removal is theologically significant?
choices: Lecture 5 already taught the modern formulation that both the Father and the Son possess tangible bodies of flesh and bone, so its removal was purely an editorial decision about length

Lecture 5 described the Father as a 'personage of spirit' and the Son as a 'personage of tabernacle,' a two-member Godhead framing later superseded by D&C 130:22, so its decanonization removed a statement no longer harmonious with developed teaching
Lecture 5 articulated the Nicene consubstantial Trinity, and it was removed because the Church had by 1921 fully rejected Trinitarianism in favor of tritheism
The Lectures were never canonical at all; their 1835 inclusion was an unauthorized printer's addition, so 1921 merely corrected a clerical error
Lecture 5 taught that the Holy Ghost is the literal spirit-mind shared between the Father and Son, which the Church preserved as official doctrine even after removing the Lectures
source: Lectures on Faith 5:2; D&C 130:22; Dialogue, 'The Lectures on Faith: A Case Study in Decanonization'; 1921 D&C committee report
notes: Correct answer captures the actual Lecture 5 language (Father 'personage of spirit,' Son 'personage of tabernacle') and the real reason for theological tension with the later corporeal-Father teaching of D&C 130:22. A inverts the history (the modern body doctrine was NOT in Lecture 5). C is an anti-Mormon caricature ('tritheism'). D is false—the 1835 conference accepted the whole volume. E is a folk reading of the Holy Ghost. Tests understanding of doctrinal development, not header trivia.

question: D&C 93:29 declares that 'intelligence, or the light of truth, was not created or made, neither indeed can be.' Joseph Smith's King Follett discourse elaborated that the intelligence of spirits had no beginning. On the precise question of WHAT was co-eternal—an undifferentiated 'intelligence' as raw material later organized into individual spirits, OR each person's individual self-existent identity from all eternity—what is the official Church position?
choices: The Church has authoritatively settled that each individual ego/identity is literally self-existent and uncreated from all eternity, per Joseph Smith and Pratt
The Church has authoritatively settled that intelligence is an undifferentiated substance that the Father later organized into distinct spirit children, per B. H. Roberts

The Church has no binding canonical resolution: both the 'intelligence-as-individual' and 'intelligence-as-material-later-organized' readings have been advanced by General Authorities, and the matter remains theologically unsettled
Scripture teaches creation ex nihilo of spirits, so the question is moot—intelligences were created by God before the Fall
The matter was settled by the 1909 First Presidency statement 'The Origin of Man,' which defined intelligence as identical to the resurrected physical body
source: D&C 93:29; Abraham 3:22; King Follett Discourse; B. H. Roberts vs. Orson Pratt debate; BYU Studies, 'The King Follett Discourse'
notes: This is a genuinely unsettled question; the correct answer reports it as non-canonical rather than picking a camp. A (Pratt/individualist) and B (Roberts/raw-material) are the two real competing GA positions offered as confident-sounding traps. D is the protestant_trap (ex nihilo, explicitly rejected by D&C 93:29 and Abr 3). E misattributes content to the 1909 statement and conflates intelligence with body. Tests the candidate's ability to recognize the limits of correlated doctrine.

question: 2 Nephi 25:23 states, 'for we know that it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.' Which reading best reflects mainstream Latter-day Saint soteriology as taught by recent apostles (e.g., Uchtdorf, Bednar) and the Book of Mormon as a whole, avoiding both works-righteousness and grace-alone errors?
choices: Grace activates only after a person has individually exhausted every possible good work and earned a baseline of merit; 'all we can do' is a quota of righteousness one must complete first
Grace is sufficient apart from any covenant obedience; 'after all we can do' is hyperbole and human effort contributes nothing to salvation

The Atonement's enabling and redeeming grace is operative throughout the disciple's life; 'after all we can do' denotes wholehearted, ongoing covenant effort and repentance, not a precondition that earns grace—we are saved by grace even as we strive
Salvation is unconditional for all who are baptized, since grace covers all sin automatically upon entry into the covenant regardless of subsequent conduct
Only the resurrection (universal salvation from physical death) is by grace; exaltation is entirely by works with no grace involved
source: 2 Nephi 25:23; 2 Nephi 2:8; Mosiah 3:17-19; Dieter F. Uchtdorf 'The Gift of Grace' (Apr 2015); David A. Bednar 'The Atonement and the Journey of Mortality'
notes: A is the classic correlation_oversimplification / works-quota misreading of 'after all we can do' that recent apostles explicitly corrected. B is the protestant_trap (grace-alone). D is a progressive/cheap-grace distortion that ignores enduring to the end. E falsely severs grace from exaltation. The correct answer captures the both/and of enabling grace plus covenant effort that distinguishes LDS soteriology from both Reformation sola gratia and works-righteousness.

question: Critics allege the Book of Mormon is anachronistic because pre-Christian Nephite prophets worship Christ by name and practice baptism centuries before the meridian of time. From within Latter-day Saint theology, what is the doctrinally correct account of this feature?
choices: It is indeed an anachronism that the Church acknowledges as Joseph Smith's nineteenth-century projection; the Book of Mormon is valued as inspired fiction rather than ancient history

The gospel of Jesus Christ and his name were revealed to prophets from the beginning; Christ's premortal identity as Jehovah was made known by revelation, so Nephite Christ-centered faith and pre-meridian baptism reflect the gospel's eternal, restored-from-Adam continuity
The Nephites worshipped a generic Messiah figure and the name 'Jesus Christ' was inserted only in Joseph Smith's translation choices, not in the underlying record

Old Testament-era peoples could not have known Christ's name; these passages prove the gold plates contained only the Law of Moses and the Christian content is the Holy Ghost speaking through the translator
Baptism and Christ-worship before the Atonement would have been efficacious only retroactively and were therefore symbolic rehearsals with no actual covenant force until after the Resurrection
source: Mosiah 3:8; 2 Nephi 25:26; Moses 6:51-52,64-68; Jacob 4:4-5; 'The gospel taught to Adam'; Bruce R. McConkie 'The Mortal Messiah'
notes: The official LDS position is that the fulness of the gospel—including faith in Christ and baptism—was had from Adam onward (Moses 6), so 'anachronism' assumes a sola-scriptura, dispensationalist progressive-revelation model the Restoration rejects. A is the progressive/inspired-fiction trap. C is an anti_mormon framing about insertion. D and E are plausible-sounding but contradict the eternal-gospel doctrine and the efficacy of pre-meridian ordinances. Tests grasp of LDS dispensationalism vs. Protestant assumptions.

question: D&C 76 describes those who become 'sons of perdition,' who alone partake of the second (spiritual) death and inherit no kingdom of glory. Considering D&C 76:31-35, the Gospel Topics teaching, and statements clarifying who qualifies, which characterization is doctrinally most precise?
choices: Anyone who commits serious sin and dies without full repentance becomes a son of perdition and inherits no glory

Sons of perdition are those who, having received a perfect knowledge by the Holy Ghost, then deny the truth and 'crucify Christ unto themselves'—an exceedingly rare condition requiring sure knowledge first; the vast majority of even grievous sinners will inherit a kingdom of glory
All those outside the covenant—the unbaptized, including those who never heard the gospel—are sons of perdition by default
The category includes all murderers and adulterers, since these sins are described as unforgivable in scripture
Sons of perdition are simply a metaphor for the wicked in general; the term carries no distinct doctrinal meaning beyond 'the lost'
source: D&C 76:31-38; D&C 132:27; Matthew 12:31-32; Joseph Smith, Teachings; Gospel Topics, 'Unpardonable Sin'
notes: The correct answer captures the high bar: perfect knowledge by the Holy Ghost followed by willful denial (the unpardonable sin against the Holy Ghost), making the category exceedingly rare. A is the Sunday-School oversimplification conflating it with serious sin. C is an anti_mormon caricature condemning the unevangelized (LDS doctrine actually offers salvation for the dead). D conflates murder/adultery (serious but not categorically unpardonable for most) with the sin against the Holy Ghost. E is a progressive/demythologizing dodge. Tests precise grasp of who qualifies and the breadth of glory available to nearly all.
